screen_policy: Every slide must prove the exact copy through visible Aachu/Zuv behavior. Any doubtful slide blocks image generation until repaired and re-reviewed.

slide_reviews.copy:
More unofficial rules of marriage
that nobody tells you

Rule no. 1
“Should we order something?”
is not a question.
The decision has already been made.

Rule no. 2
If one person asks, “Kahan hai?”
The other must find it
without being told what “it” is.

Rule no. 3
Old screenshots
do not have an expiry date.
They can be presented as evidence
at any time.

Rule no. 4
The person who did not pack
will always ask,
“Charger rakh liya?”
Usually when you’re already in the cab.

Rule no. 5
Wi-Fi starts working
the moment your spouse enters the room.
Nobody knows why.

Rule no. 6
Midnight hunger
is never one person’s emergency.
The entire house gets activated.

Rule no. 7
Every unnecessary purchase
begins immediately after
a serious conversation
about saving money.

Rule no. 8
Nobody is actually in charge.
Both just keep showing up.
Usually saying, “Maine bola tha.”

review_provenance.raw_response:
Produced before seeing any copy or intent and based only on the nine blind storyboard cards.

1. Two adults prepare for travel in a familiar home, working separately but comfortably together, evidenced by the open suitcase, clothes search, mugs, stepped-over charging cable, and exchanged glance.
2. The couple makes a shared food choice with one partner already anticipating the other’s request, evidenced by the asking gesture, visible dish selection, and both bodies leaning toward one phone.
3. One partner urgently searches for keys already dangling from their own hand while the other points out the mistake, creating affectionate comedy through the visible keyring, pointing hand, and interrupted search.
4. One partner calmly presents old messages while the other becomes defensively sheepish, suggesting playful accountability through the turned phone, frozen hand, and amused expression, though the exact dispute is unreadable.
5. Mid-departure beside a waiting cab, both realize a charger remains plugged inside, evidenced by the loaded bags, open doorway, nearly empty-handed partner, and synchronized turn toward the wall socket.
6. After one partner struggles with the hotel router, connectivity appears as the other enters and shrugs, evidenced by the crouched troubleshooting posture, steady router lights, connected laptop symbol, and incredulous look-up, though causality is unclear.
7. Both partners suddenly coordinate a late-night food plan, evidenced by one comparing phone choices while the other pulls on slippers and empties snacks onto the bed, with both bodies aimed toward the same task.
8. The couple jointly carries an oversized impulsive market purchase with equal guilt and delight, evidenced by each supporting one end of the lamp and exchanging matched looks.
9. Returning home, they simultaneously catch the slipping lamp and laugh in mutual blame, evidenced by the repeated threshold, shared rescue, shoulder-to-shoulder pointing, travel bags, and recovered charger.

Sequence: A familiar couple moves from parallel travel preparation through shared mistakes, teasing, improvisation, and an impractical purchase to a synchronized, affectionate return home.

Weaknesses: Frame 4’s exact incident and connection to the trip are unclear, Frame 6 lacks a visible cause for the connection change, and Frame 7 partially repeats Frame 2’s phone-and-food behavior.

Verdict: PASS—the travel continuity and progression from separate activity to shared complicity and simultaneous action make this a coherent relationship story rather than disconnected scenes.
